content.comment_body: Hello, I have an encoder connected to my [product_name] ([article_no]). It's used to measure the distance through my stroke harvester. I'm using I5 and I6 as inputs, and everything seems to work during manual and slower testing. For every 100 cm, I observe 300 pulses when moving slowly, but in actual operation, I see far fewer pulses. Does anyone know why this happens and how to resolve it?
How much time does it actually take to cover 100 cm?

Hello [user_name], Based on your description, your sensor is likely an incremental encoder. These only work reliably at low pulse frequencies; otherwise, [product_name] may be too slow to register all pulses. Regards, [user_name] (translated with Google)

Hi, Estimating, it takes about one second to cover 100 cm (one stroke equals ~100 cm). The [product_name] display counts 100 per measure wheel turn, and 300 for each 100 cm. You can refer to this video for details: [url] Regards, [user_name]

Hello! That’s not ideal. Is it possible to use an encoder that provides fewer pulses per 360-degree rotation? I want measurements that are as accurate as possible, but even if the system reads 310 cm instead of 305 cm, it's still usable. What type of encoder would be suitable for this measuring function? This video might clarify what I am aiming for: [url] Regards, [user_name]

Hello [user_name], What matters isn’t the total number of pulses per encoder rotation but the number of pulses your [product_name] receives per second. The input frequency capacity is not very high (refer to the manual). Quick input options in some versions do not help much due to internal processing limits. This topic has already been thoroughly discussed in the forum, but perhaps a similar post in the German section could assist you. Regards, [user_name] (translated with Google)

Hi [user_name], Does this mean it’s not possible to measure centimeters as intended, even if switching to another encoder? I know that some users use [product_name] [version_no] for similar applications. Regards, [user_name]

Hello everyone, First, convert RPM to Pulses. For example: if the RPM is 600, then it's 10 rotations per second. If the encoder generates 500 pulses per cycle, that’s 5000 pulses per second or 5 kHz. For inputs I3, I4, I5, and I6 designated for fast counting (only certain [product_name] [version_no] models), the maximum is 5 kHz if the fast input is directly connected to the counter function block. Sincerely,

analysis.insight_summary: The core issue is pulse loss at higher speeds when using [product_name] ([version_no]) with an incremental encoder for distance measurement. Manual and slow operations provide correct counts, but fast real-world use results in missed pulses due to the hardware’s limited input frequency capability. The main concern is the product's insufficient speed for real-time, high-frequency pulse counting, leading to unreliable measurements for applications that require faster data acquisition.
analysis.user_expectations: The user expects [product_name] to reliably and accurately count high-frequency encoder pulses in real time, providing precise distance measurements for their equipment, regardless of operational speed.
